speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROBLEMS CONSIDERED AND PROGRAMME FOR FUTURE ACTION-REPORT TABLED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 8,
I stated, in reply to a question by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon), that I would table the report of the united and associated nations conference on food and agriculture as soon as it was available, and that, at the same time, I would make a brief general statement on the work of the conference and the programme for future action. I now table the report as approved on June 3, under the designation: Final Act.
The food conference was held at Hot Springs, Virginia. Its sessions opened on May 18, and were concluded on June 3. It was the first general conference of the united nations. That in itself gives the conference an historic significance. While the conference met in time of war, it was not concerned with the prosecution of the war. It had to do with one of the problems which demand solution if, after the termination of hostilities, the world is to enjoy enduring peace. Its purpose was to assist in freeing the peoples of the world from want, once the axis powers have been defeated. The conference was an act of faith in the continuing solidarity of the united nations.
The fact that the subject matter of the conference was food and agriculture is evidence of a determination to make a fundamental approach to the solution of post-war problems. No subject could have been more suitable for exploration. The production of food is the most important of man's economic activities. Its absorbs the energies of more men and women than all other economic pursuits combined.
A consideration of the problems falls naturally into three parts: the objectives in quantity and quality tn be set in the consumption of food; the production of foodstuffs to meet consumption needs; the better distribution of the produce of agriculture and of fisheries.
The conference recognized that there had never been enough food produced in the world to maintain the health of all its peoples. The development of the science of nutrition has added greatly to the knowledge of the kinds of food needed to maintain health and efficiency. The nutrition experts who were gathered at the conference set the goals for the achievement of better standards of health, and indicated various measures which might be taken to that end, particularly the provisions of protective and other nutritionally desirable foods. The problem to be faced was stated by the conference to be that of ensuring the production of the necessary food and having it made available to the consumer. The primary emphasis in all the studies made by

Food Conference
the nutrition experts, and the basic conclusion of the conference itself was that the production of food must be increased if freedom from want is to be achieved.
The conference gave attention to methods of increasing the supiply of food by such means as raising the efficiency of production, the employment of additional land and labour, the conservation of resources,, and the advantages to be derived, in certain cases, from international specialization.
The largest market for the produce of agriculture lies amongst the tillers of the soil. Producers of food are also important consumers of other goods as well as of their own produce. It was recognized by the conference that the general welfare would be promoted by ensuring to the producers of food a reasonable return for their labour. The conference therefore considered special measures to increase the purchasing power of agriculturists generally, and, particularly, the purchasing power of the less advanced and less favoured peoples.
A second main conclusion of the conference was that the expansion of agricultural production must be part of the expansion of the whole world economy. It was recognized that if markets are to be opened for an expanded food production, and if people are to be able to buy the food which they need, poverty must be made to disappear. The increasing of industrial production, the provision of full employment, the prevention of exploitation, the development of social legislation, the orderly management of currencies and investments, the fostering of international trade through the reduction of trade barriers, were seen to be problems to be considered if the purposes of the conference on food and agriculture were to be realized. These studies lay outside the scope of the conference and call for separate consideration, which some of them are already receiving.
The conference was primarily concerned with agriculture, but it did not overlook the value, as foodstuffs, of fish and marine products. It recognized the importance of fish in the economy of many countries. It recommended that the general conclusions which it had reached, wherever appropriate, should apply to fish and marine products.
In its deliberations, the conference had to take account of the special world conditions under which it was meeting. There were two questions of great importance which did not come within its terms of reference. The first concerns the production of food and its distribution in wartime, which is a task for

agencies already in existence. The second is the question of relief, on an international scale, which is to be the subject of a conference at an early date.
The conference's study of the problems of food and agriculture was partly concerned with the intermediate period between the present, and the time when the long-term goals of the conference could be actively pursued and achieved.
Countries which are free from the tyranny of the invader are already able to take steps towards the attainment of the goals set at the conference. As other countries are liberated, they, too, can strive towards these goals. The immediate aim must be the abolition of hunger as a first step towards freedom from want. During the transition period which will follow the cessation of hostilities in particular areas, measures will have to be taken to meet the special circumstances caused by the war. Long-term goals will have to be kept firmly in mind so that temporary expedients will not result in permanent maladjustments.
Throughout its deliberations, the conference recognized the primary responsibility of each nation to ensure that its own people are fully employed, and that they have the means of procuring the food needed for a healthy life. The conference also agreed that only through active cooperation with other nations can the fullest prosperity of each nation be secured.
The final act of the conference, the result of its deliberations, comprises a declaration and some thirty resolutions. In the first resolution, the conference recommends that all nations represented should set out in a formal declaration their individual obligation to their own people, and to one another, to collaborate in raising the levels of nutrition and standards of living of their peoples, and in improving the efficient production and distribution of agricultural products. It also recommends that they report to one another on the progress achieved. Other resolutions contain statements of principles and recommendations of policy for the short-term and the long-term period. The resolutions also dealt with the opening up of undeveloped areas suitable for settlement and food production, the fostering of desirable changes in the pattern of production designed to give greater emphasis to protective foods; the provision of agricultural credit; the advancement of cooperative societies, and the improvement of marketing facilities. I need scarcely assure the house that all these recommendations will receive detailed study by the government.
To facilitate collaboration among nations in this field of endeavour, the conference

Agriculture Committee Report
recommended that a permanent international organization on food and agriculture be established. It suggested that each government represented at the conference appoint a representative to an interim commission, the duty of which would be to carry out the recommendations of the conference and to prepare a specific plan for a permanent international organization on food and agriculture. The conference invited the President of the United States of America to arrange for the establishment of this interim commission, and for the calling of an early meeting.
In recommending the functions of the proposed permanent organization, the conference followed closely the comprehensive agenda which had been fixed for its own deliberations. It also urged the interim commission to give consideration to the question of providing for membership in the permanent organization of countries not represented at the conference. It recommended as well the association of the permanent organization with other institutions, which already exist, or which may be set up later, in the field of food and agriculture, and in related scientific, economic and other fields.
President Roosevelt in his speech to the delegates on Monday last, described the conference as "epoch making". He willingly accepted the recommendation that, as President of the United States, he should call together the proposed interim commission.
The president associated himself with the declaration of the conference that every nation should assume the responsibility, in collaboration with others, of providing adequate food for its own people. I am prepared to make at once a similar declaration on behalf of Canada.
In conclusion, I should like to mention among other of the promising results of the first united nations conference, the friendly spirit which inspired its deliberations, the earnestness with which the delegates worked together toward worthy ends, and the unanimity with which their decisions were reached. .
Mr. Speaker, I should ask that copies of the Final Act be provided to members of the house, and would move, seconded by Mr. Crerar:
That 700 copies in English and 300 copies in French of the Final Act of the united nations conference on food and agriculture, laid on the table this day, be printed forthwith, and that standing order 64 in relation thereto be suspended.
At first glance, it would seem that seven hundred copies in English and three hundred in French of the Final Act may not be as large a number as would be desired. I am informed however that something in the nature of an abridged popular statement which will serve all immediate purposes will shortly be available, and I think this would be a sufficient number, therefore, of copies of the Final Act in its formal shape to be obtained.

speechtext: Mr. THOMAS REID (New Westminster) moved the first reading of Bill No. 109 (from the senate) to incorporate Bethel Full Gospel Assembly.

subtopic: BETHEL . FULL GOSPEL ASSEMBLY
speechtext: I would ask the hon. member to give a full explanation of this bill.

subtopic: BETHEL . FULL GOSPEL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
I should be glad to give a full explanation if we had time, but probably that would take all afternoon. I shall give a short resume, however, of what it means, and perhaps that will suffice until the bill comes before the committee. Those asking for the incorporation of the church have their headquarters in Vancouver. They are part of a sect whose headquarters are located in the state of Tennessee, which state is well known to all hon. members of this house. They have been in existence for some forty years. Their teachings are those of the new testament; their beliefs are similar to those of the Baptists. They desire incorporation in order to administer the affairs of the church, including real property. Their object is the dissemination of the gospel in all languages, the ordination of ministers and missionaries, the establishment of schools; and as a Presbyterian I am pleased to help the church along.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: MOVEMENT OF FARM WORKERS FROM THE PRAIRIES TO ONTARIO

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MOVEMENT OF FARM WORKERS FROM THE PRAIRIES TO ONTARIO
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, will the Minister of Labour kindly amplify his statement made last night with respect to the proposed movement of 1,000 farm workers from the prairies to Ontario for temporary farm wTork this summer, and explain particularly why such workers will be obliged to bear any part of their transportation costs?

subtopic: MOVEMENT OF FARM WORKERS FROM THE PRAIRIES TO ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker; owing to the
advance in farm work in Saskatchewan it has been possible to make an arrangement whereby workers will be brought east to [DOT] Ontario to help out during an urgent period. They will be assigned to farms mainly in central and southwestern Ontario.
To begin with the movement will be of about 500 men and the maximum transfer will be 1,000 men. The dominion government will pay transportation costs easterly but will require workers to pay a small amount of the return trip westerly.
It is expected these western men will stay in Ontario about two months, but certainly they will be back on the prairies in time for the western harvest. No man will be recruited in the west whose absence would interfere with farm production there. I hope we shall have completed arrangements for this transfer of farm labour within the next ten days as the help is needed in Ontario now.
W. W. Dawson, supervisor of farm labour requirements for Saskatchewan and director of the dominion-provincial farm labour programme for that province, has advised

Labour Conditions
that because of the good work of "win the war" municipal committees there actually will be men to spare from Saskatchewan farms from now until harvest time. On May 28 he wrote a report to one of my officials, and I quote this paragraph:
You will certainly hear from us if we get stuck for help, but in the meantime I think it is safe to say that we have the farm labour problem under control in the province, and it is my expectation that within te,n days we will have more men than we know what to do with.

subtopic: MOVEMENT OF FARM WORKERS FROM THE PRAIRIES TO ONTARIO
speechtext: In the slack season?

subtopic: MOVEMENT OF FARM WORKERS FROM THE PRAIRIES TO ONTARIO
speechtext: Yes, that is obvious.

subtopic: MOVEMENT OF FARM WORKERS FROM THE PRAIRIES TO ONTARIO
speechtext: Who says that?

subtopic: MOVEMENT OF FARM WORKERS FROM THE PRAIRIES TO ONTARIO
speechtext: Dawson. I read that passage because it has a western tinge to it.

subtopic: MOVEMENT OF FARM WORKERS FROM THE PRAIRIES TO ONTARIO
speechtext: I do not know what it means.

subtopic: MOVEMENT OF FARM WORKERS FROM THE PRAIRIES TO ONTARIO
speechtext:
I will say it is the way practical people deal with a practical problem. Put it that way.
It is for this reason that we are seeking men from Saskatchewan. On Saturday afternoon an official of the labour department called the minister of agriculture of Manitoba by telephone in order to advise him of the plan for bringing some men east from Saskatchewan. The Minister of Agriculture was out of the city but the whole matter was placed before the deputy minister of agriculture, Mr. J. H. Evans. Mr. Evans said that the matter would be fully discussed at a special meeting of the dominion-provincial committee on farm labour to see what possibility there might be to participate in the plan so far as Manitoba is concerned. This meeting will be held to-morrow morning, June 15, and Mr. Evans will advise us immediately as to the conclusions of that meeting.
The deputy minister of agriculture for Alberta, Mr. O. 8. Longman, who is also chairman of the dominion-provincial committee on farm labour, has been advised of the plan. Because of the distance of Alberta from Ontario no specific request has been made for sending Alberta farmers east. It was however pointed out to Mr. Longman that word has been received from British Columbia of a very serious shortage of help to put up hay in the interior. If there were some men from Alberta who might be spared for five or six weeks between now and harvest time, Mr. Longman was asked to consider the possibility of organizing some movement into this area of British Columbia.
With reference to the particular point raised by the leader of the opposition (Mr. 
Graydon) we decided to require part payment of transportation costs in order to ensure the bona fides -of the men wishing to come east. Our experience in the past has been that when free transportation is offered there are some who simply go along for the trip and make themselves scarce on arrival. It is not expected that in each case the charge will be more than five dollars.

subtopic: POSTPONEMENT DURING HOSTILITIES-PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: POSTPONEMENT DURING HOSTILITIES-PROPOSED AMENDMENT TO BRITISH NORTH AMERICA ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement to the house with respect to the subject of redistribution which has been mentioned on one or two previous occasions. The statement has a bearing upon the length of time it may take parliament to conclude the work of the present session. On more than one occasion my colleagues and I have given anxious consideration to the problems involved in undertaking, during the war, the work of readjustment of the representation in the House of Commons. I need not remind hon. members who have had a long experience in the house that the process of redistribution may give rise to sharp and even acrimonious differences. The government is desirous, as I know the house and the country are, to avoid, in war time, occasions for political differences and controversy, whenever such differences can be avoided without prejudice to the national war effort or to the effective functioning of our free parliamentary institutions.
We are particularly anxious to prevent differences that might be avoided arising at a time when hostilities, in which our own Canadian forces may be engaged, are at an acute stage. From now on until the close of the war it will at no time be possible to predict what the actual situation may be. We may

Redistribution

be certain, however, that until victory over the axis powers is finally achieved, the situation will become increasingly intense. Apart altogether from future possibilities, circumstances arising out of the war have occasioned special difficulties in respect to redistribution during the continuance of hostilities.
In the first place, the census of 1941, on which the redistribution would have to be based, was taken after Canada had been at war for almost two years. In that period, enlistments in the armed forces, migrations from province to province occasioned by the establishment of war industries, and other shifts of population directly attributable to war-time conditions, had abnormally added to the numbers in some provinces and decreased those in others. In the two years that have elapsed since the census was taken, war-time movements of population have continued and may even have intensified. It may be questioned therefore whether a redistribution based upon the situation in 1941 would conform at all closely to the actual situation which would prevail when the time came to hold a general election. There is another important circumstance of w'hich I am sure all members of the house will wish to take account. Redistribution involves not merely the readjustment of the representation of the provinces, but also the delimitation of the electoral divisions within all or nearly all of the provinces.
I need not remind hon. members that a considerable number of our fellow members are absent on active service in the armed forces and that some of them are overseas. Redistribution, affecting, as it inevitably would, the boundaries of a great many constituencies, would be a matter of immediate concern to them, and a matter on which their right to express their views should, if at all possible, be preserved. These considerations have caused the government to conclude that it does not now seem desirable that readjustment of representation on the basis of the census of 1941 should have to be made during the continuance of the hostilities in which Canada is now engaged, and that an amendment to the British North America Act should be sought in order to permit of the postponement of redistribution.
My colleague the Minister of Justice will at an early date introduce the appropriate resolution in this house. A similar resolution will be introduced in the other house. I believe that the course the government is

recommending will, upon careful consideration, commend itself to members of all parties in the house, as I am sure it will to the people of Canada generally. It will be recognized that the government is seeking to have done only what is in the national interest at a time of war, and that by limiting the effect of the action proposed to the period of hostilities in which Canada is now engaged there will be no occasion for the slightest apprehension that any fundamental constitutional rights will be affected.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, June 11, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to his majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the Chair.

War Appropriation-Supplies
1.	Additions and extensions to plants, $195,000,000.

Mr. Chairman, I listened this afternoon to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) announcing to the house the attitude which he felt should characterize hon. members of this house during war time, and I could not help but think that if we all were to adopt the standards suggested by him considerable improvement would take place, not only in the debates in this parliament but in the contribution that each and all of us are endeavouring to make. I feel that the duty of an opposition in approaching a discussion of the various matters under the war appropriation measure, should be divided in two parts: one, to give credit when credit is due, and the other, fearlessly to point out shortcomings or deficiencies to the end that Canada's war effort may reach a point of maximization at the earliest possible time.
As I listened to the recital of the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) on Friday last, I could not help following with great interest and with great pride, what he had to say for without regard to political party the members of this house are Canadians first and foremost, and all will experience pride in the production record of Canadian war industry as revealed by him. It means an economic revolution in Canada has taken place in the transformation of Canada into one of the great industrial nations of the world. It represents a change of attitude and a change of emphasis, with each of the united nations concentrating on the production of that which they can most conveniently produce. It represents the beginning of the culmination of the results of the combined production and resources board which was set up in November, 1942. The duties of the board were defined as follows:
The board shall combine the production programmes of the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada, into a single integrated programme adjusted to the strategic requirements of the war as indicated to the board by the combined chiefs of staff and to all relevant production factors. In this connection the board shall take account of the need for maximum utilization of the productive resources available to the United States, the British commonwealth of nations and the united nations, the need to reduce demands on shipping to a minimum, and the essential needs of the civilian populations.
Canada's production record in the past year, and I speak as one who ini the past
72537-228}
has been, most critical, is a tribute to what private initiative and private enterprise can do in this country with state collaboration. During the last few months tremendous, drastic and far-reaching changes have taken place in production, and they are indicated in the estimates placed before the house by the minister. Canada in company with the other united nations has adopted the uniform principle of producing offensive weapons instead of defensive weapons. The blueprint of victory consists in taking the offensive. Besides the production of ordinary munitions Canada will concentrate on the production of certain types of aircraft, nine in number, particularly Lancaster bombers and Mosquito bombers, and on fighting naval vessels and on cargo vessels. There has been a change in ground production, due in large measure I am informed to the experience of our troops at Dieppe and in Africa during recent months. I am not going into the question of manpower to-day, but the change in ground production will mean either unemployment for many thousands of men in Canada or the hoarding by industry of men until changed conditions make them, employable unless action is taken and immediately by selective service authorities to the end that these men be placed in their proper positions.
Women have made a great contribution in munitions production, but they are not as yet being used to the extent that they are in Great Britain and the United States of America in industry. Recently a number of members of this house had an opportunity to visit the city of Buffalo and to see there in operation two of the greatest aircraft plants in the United States producing fighting planes. From information secured there I can tell the house, and what I say now will be confirmed by those who were present on that visit, that some fifty-two per cent of the employees in one of these great factories are women. We in Canada will have to increase the number of women in industry if the man-power requirements of the army, the navy and the air force and of industry are to be supplied.
In the past, in 1940, 1941 and 1942, Canada as a member of the united nations found out that valour without production would not win victory. The experience of recent days in Africa and of very recent days in the islands of the Mediterranean has shown the necessity for ever-increasing air power on the part of the united nations. There are many to-day who will contend that, having regard to the
War Appropriation-Supplies

vast destruction being wrought each night in the great industrial cities of the Ruhr and other parts of Germany, the united nations should devote themselves almost exclusively to developing great air power; that overwhelming air power can and will bring Germany and the other axis nations to their knees.
When I offer words of criticism, as I shall shortly, they will be directed to only one or two matters and my colleagues will devote themselves to other phases in connection with, production. The record in the production of cargo-carrying ships is one in which this opposition takes pride, as the idea was first forcefully brought before this house, by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), and the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black). We take pride in the production of tanks and the contribution they have made in Russia, and we also recall that when one of the members on this side of the house first suggested that tanks could and should be built in Canada-I refer to the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce), and I have his actual words here-the attitude taken by the government was that it could not be done.

That statement has been made several times. Will the hon. member read the words where the government said it could not be done? The government had been working on tanks for months before it was mentioned here.
I will give the words.
Never mind the oratory-give us the words.

There is a peculiar trait in the minister-as long as you praise him he is perfectly satisfied, but once you offer constructive criticism immediately he becomes aroused. I will give him the quotation later.
Why not now?

In effect, the minister ridiculed the idea, and five days later one of the departments of information announced that Canada was going ahead very shortly with the production of 300 tanks. No doubt the only objection the minister had at that time, knowing as he must have known that Canada was going to go ahead with the production of tanks, was that the suggestion had come from the opposition before he himself had made the announcement.
I think that we have justifiable pride in what has been done in that it does show one

thing that cannot too often be accentuated in this country and among democracies, and that is that democracies do function when challenged by danger. They are slow to begin operations but when once the people of democracies appreciate that they are fighting for the survival of freedom great results ensue. The results in the united nations are such that within less than four years they are to-day producing more war supplies than the axis nations, who started seven or nine years prior to the war to produce. The united nations have caught up with them in the interval since the beginning of the war and have now passed them.
A tribute should be paid to the Canadian industrialists and to labour for their partnership in this great work. There is not a man or woman in Canada to-day who, in the production record as outlined by the minister, has not a sense of pride in the fact that, through their contributions to victory loans and their actual labour in our factories, and through the leadership in trade unions and the cooperation of industry itself and industrialists, outstanding results have been achieved. They all have pride in their participation in this partnership of patriotic production, which will pay dividends in assured victory for our armed forces of the united nations.
Labour in Canada has a record of which it might well be proud. When I was in Buffalo I was told that a recent survey had taken place in the United States in regard to the question of, shall I call it, unjustifiable absenteeism, absenteeism that is not justified by necessity. In eight of the greatest cities of the United States, industrial centres, the rate of absenteeism was found to be from five to-fifteen per cent with an average of around nine per cent compared with two per cent prior to the war. Translated into production that represents tremendous figures in potential output. Here in Canada, according to the best figures I have been able to secure, *we find that in spite of the fact that there is heavy taxation on all those engaged in labour and that therefore some may be poorer if they work six days in the week than if they work four, absenteeism during the past year has been less than the low rate of two per cent in the United States prior to the W'ar. That tells its own story and clearly proves that labour in Canada in general appreciates everything that this war is being fought for; it appreciates what it means to labour as to all others.

War Appropriation-Supplies
I think it is a matter of pride to all Canadians that while wages are maintained in the main as of October, 1941, and that across the line in the United States wages are immeasurably greater, in munitions and war production the men and women of this country have continued, regardless of their feelings with regard to the wages they receive, to contribute to the great work that they have done in the production of this nation.
We want the minister to be able to place before the house the record of the numbers of men who will be out of work in each industry by changes that are being made. What transfers are being made in consequence now and what will be made? We also want to know the plans the government have to prevent anyone in industry from hoarding employees against the day when production has been resumed in that particular industry.
I come now to a question on which I think the government must give particulars, that of capital advances and assistance to private companies, and the matter of the continuance of government corporations after the war. Last year and the year before I asked the minister what were the plans and what was intended to be done and what disposal is to be made of these plants after the war. After almost four years of war, the answer given in past years will not be accepted as sufficient to-day. The general answer given then was to the effect that no plans had been made and no decision arrived at. When I look at the record and find that Canada has advanced by way of capital assistance to private corporations the sum of $821,000,000 as of December last and that 335 private companies have received capital assistance, having regard to the expenditure that has been made in this direction and the vast developments that have taken place, the building of tremendous factories and the installation of machinery that has run into literally hundreds of millions of dollars, I feel that the people of Canada have a right to know now what the government's plan is for the disposal of these industries after the war.
So far as I have been able to find out, all that has been done in this connection has been to provide optional purchase clauses in some, but very few, of the government agreements with private corporations. In a return, No. 298 of May 21, 1943, answers are given to questions asked by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). The hon. member asked the following question: Are there any optional purchase clauses contained in government agreements with private corporations in connection with government investments in any industry or plant? The list is given there. There is a number of agreements, with Defence Industries Limited, Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company Limited, Alberta Nitrogen Company, Electric Reduction Company of Canada Limited, Canada Wire and Cable Company, Anaconda American Brass Limited, Nichols Chemical Company Limited, Electric Steels Limited, Chemical Construction Corporation and Welland Chemical Works Limited, Shawinigan Chemicals Limited, Macdonald Chemicals Limited, Naugatuck Chemicals Limited. Defence Industries Limited has received capital advances of about $109,000,000, and these other companies have received capital advances totalling, according to approximate figuring, about $170,000,000. In these agreements there is not the definiteness there should be. The general provision relative to the disposal of plants seems to be, as indicated in relation to Defence Industries Limited, that the government shall give the company a sixty-day option to purchase the plant or any part thereof at a price it is willing to accept from any other party; if the offer is not accepted, the government is free to sell the plant to any other party at a price not less than that offered to Defence Industries Limited. These terms are not clear; indeed they are so wide open that the government is left in a position where a sale far below the proper and fair price could be made. The criticism that I have heard and which I am bringing before the minister is based on the fact that the government now is not making arrangements to protect the interests of the people of Canada after the war for the tremendous amounts they have expended in war industry. I believe the time has come, in view of the large expenditure which will be made this year, estimated at $195,000,000, in additions to and extensions of plants, that we in western Canada have the right to share in the industrialization which is taking place.
I will cite as an example the province of Saskatchewan. We could have tanneries established there, but our hide production is shipped out of the province to be manufactured. We are in a position to manufacture glycerine and glue, yet only a few months ago an arrangement was made whereby we would ship the bones out of Saskatchewan to the United States of America, where they are manufactured into one or other of these components. I do not want to become parochial, but I must again bring to the minister's attention the fact that,
War Appropriation-Supplies

according to the most reliable figures I have been able to obtain, of the vast sum of $800,000,000 dispensed by way of capital assistance, Saskatchewan has received less than $1,000,000. There is no justification for that. The hon. member for Saskatoon City (Mr. Bence) has dealt with the question of establishing a flax processing plant in western Canada and plants for the production of synthetic rubber. Factories could and should be established in various parts of Canada to provide when the war is over a backlog for the unemployment which may otherwise take place. It is a notoriously well-known fact that man-power does not move freely back and forth across the dominion where work is available, and seeks employment as near home as it can.
The following inquiries were directed to the Minister of Munitions and Supply, reference sessional paper 231-C, March 29, 1943: "In each province, what is the total amount of capital assistance given?. What is the total volume of all orders given by the Department of Munitions and Supply (a) to all Canadian industry and (b) in each province?" The answer, which I do not accept because ordinary addition will bring out the necessary facts, is that "it is impossible to give a money break-down by provinces that will properly reveal the extent to which each province is participating in war orders made possible by capital assistance or by the operation of crown companies or by ordinary award of contracts". With all due respect, I say that that statement does not represent the facts. The only reason I can suggest why the minister failed to give an answer showing what each province has received compared with what other provinces received, is that the record was anything but favourable to governmental planning. The United States today, passing through a similar condition to our own here in Canada, realizing that when the war is over she will own or be interested in factories valued at many thousands of millions of dollars, is engaged in a survey with a view of ascertaining what plans can be and should be made now for the disposal of these plants after the war. I do not know what the figures are for Canada; I have endeavoured to secure them but I have been unable to do so; but in the United States, when the war is over, the government will own 96 per cent of the new shipbuilding industries; 93 per cent of the new aircraft industries; 71 per cent of the new iron and steel plants, and 64 per cent of the electrical equipment factories. No doubt a similar situation obtains in this country. fMr. Diefenbaker.]
We in parliament have a right to a declaration this session on this problem. Will these industrial undertakings be leased, or will they be sold to private enterprise, subject to the necessary controls to assure that monopolistic enterprise shall not thereby be built up? On the other side of the picture is socialization or state operation. What is the plan of the government? Shall it be private enterprise, with the government having something to do with management? Shall it be private enterprise without any control? Or will the government continue after the war to operate some of the government-owned or war-financed plants manufacturing commodities which are as necessary in time of peace as they are in time of war? I think that in the distribution of these plants after the war, division among the different "enter-preneurs" should be made on proper terms and with the design of promoting competition. If there is one argument we hear to-day more than another it is that when the war is over the government will be in a position to turn over these plants to its friends, and to discriminate in their disposal or dispersion. That sort of argument can be and must be answered now. In the interests of post-war employment and for the good of our people as a whole a decision and a plan must be evolved now.
So far as this party is concerned its policy has been enunciated by its leader, Mr. John Bracken, and it is simply this. "While paying a tribute to what private enterprise has done and can do, and recognizing that it has been a mainspring of world progress throughout the generations, we hold that it does not and must not be allowed to mean the rampage of uncontrolled greed. Prosperity comes from production, production from enterprise, largely private enterprise. It is when enterprise fails that prosperity disappears." So far as the government of the United States is concerned there is some suggestion to-day that cooperation between industry and labour will continue when the war is over, but cooperation between industry and the government must never be substituted for competition. To-day Britain is facing this problem; and though the minister may laugh the fact remains that this is one problem which must be faced now.
I should like my hon. friend to withdraw that remark, because I was not laughing at anything the hon. gentleman said; it was at a comment made behind me.

Very well; I am quite prepared to accept that.

War Appropriation-Supplies
I do not like that to appear in my hon. friend's speech, because I was not laughing at anything he said.

I am trying to offer a serious suggestion to the minister, and I find that he usually accepts suggestions made in that way.
I have dealt with this matter at some length, and my time is nearly up. I am not going into the details of the plan for the demobilization of industry, or to offer any suggestions in that regard, but plans for this demobilization must be made now, and if I may I would suggest that the government must take into consideration the following points:
1.	A determination of the basis upon which sale or disposition shall be made.
2.	A government plan now for the conversion of these war-time industries to peacetime economy and production.
3.	A determination now as to which plants will be continued after the war for standby purposes.
4. A plan now of assistance to small industries after the war by way of loans to stimulate the change from the war-time to peace-time economy, coupled with technical advice as to the most appropriate use of their facilities in peace-time production.
We have many large industries in Canada, but in the main the backbone of our industry is the small enterprise. I have the exact figures on my desk, though I do not see them at the moment; as nearly as I remember them, however, there are only 172 industries in Canada employing more than 500 men, while there are 24,600 employing less than 500 men. There should be a guarantee that private enterprise of the small business type will receive a fair and reasonable share of the available facilities, to the end that *competition will be engendered and control of the great industries that have been *established during the war or have increased in importance since the beginning of the war shall not fall into the hands of cartels or monopoly groups. In that connection I would point out that the national planning board of the United States of America has suggested that so far as certain great industries are concerned, producing such crucial commodities as magnesium, aluminum, aircraft and the like, consideration should be given to the extension of a joint private and governmental partnership in those industries, necessary as they are to peace as to war economy.
That in general is the information I should like to secure from the minis^r in connection with this phase of his estimates. I should like to know what further extensions of existing companies are planned for this coming year. I should like to know why the provinces which up to the present time have not received any appreciable share of industry should not have an opportunity to build up some of the industrial life that is to be found in other parts of Canada, through the development of power where that power is available, in the province of Saskatchewan for an example.
In the few moments still at my disposal I want to refer to one other matter, though I shall deal with it at greater length later on;
I have reference to the production of aircraft in this country. I have before me the various speeches in this connection made by the minister, together with the reports he has given during the last three years, and all I can say is that the hopes expressed in regard to aircraft production have not been fulfilled. I go back to 1940 and find the same hopeful expressions in regard to the production of aircraft that we hear to-day, and it was the same in 1941 and 1942. On October 3, 1941, Mr. Bell, the controller, during the course of a speech, said that at that time Canada was producing more aircraft per week than in a whole year before the war, but he did not say what year he was talking about. The production before the war was shown by the minister on May 22, 1940, to have been very small. If increasing aircraft production is necessary, as apparently it is; if the war production of Germany can be reduced by seventeen per cent in three months through air attack, should not Canada now embark upon an ever-extending campaign for the production of aircraft? The record in this connection is such, I think, that an explanation is required from the minister in regard to what happened at the Malton plant when it was operated by National Steel Car. Last year and the year before it was held up as an example of efficiency in production. The people of Canada have a right to know how much money was put into that plant and what was the cost in man hours of the production of each type of aeroplane. Apparently the de Havilland plant in production of Mosquito bombers has revealed weaknesses, though members of this house have no knowledge of what happened, except that a government controller was put in charge in place of the former management. What is the production now of de Havilland Mosquitos-and1 I know

one must always ask that question subject to security neefas. The hon. Mr. Davis said two months ago in Australia that Canada was producing five Mosquito planes per day.

Mr. Chairman, those of us who listened to the speech of the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) on Friday last, and others who have since read his speech in Hansard, must have come to the conclusion that the record of achievement by the minister as it appears in Hansard is one of which every one of us can be proud. Before the war, in certain countries Canada had been looked upon as an agricultural land. To-day such is not the case, because Canada now ranks among the foremost nations of the world as an industrial producer. Some considerable credit is due the minister, and I was pleased indeed when at the opening of his remarks the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) paid his respects to the record, to the minister and to the men who have helped to produce guns, tanks and all the implements of war we are to-day producing.
I have not always seen eye to eye with the Minister of Munitions and Supply. We have had our differences. But I have never had any doubt that he was the best man this country could have obtained for the job. I think every hon. member will agree with that statement. If there are those who would not agree, I challenge them to name anyone in Canada who could better his record. The minister has had a job to do. I have differed with him, as have other hon. members from the eastern and western provinces, particularly those from British Columbia. We have differed with him in the matter of the centralization of industry in the two central provinces. As I say, we realize that the minister had a job to do, that he had to produce these articles of war, but I am just wondering if after the war the eastern and western provinces, particularly British Columbia, will have any opportunity to develop industries. It may well be that by that time we might be over-industrialized in certain lines of endeavour.
I am not going to deal with a great number of matters this afternoon, but there is one thing I should like to bring to the attention of the committee and of the Minister of Munitions and Supply. I refer to the production of steel in British Columbia. I may say right here that I do not approach this subject as one who is ignorant of the facts. I am one of the few members of the house who have had practical and successful 72537-229
experience in the manufacture and production of both steel and iron. As the minister pointed out, we are producing in Canada at the present time some 3,000,000 tons of steel. We are importing 2,000,000 tons, with the possibility that we shall have to import
500,000	tons additional this year. I wonder how many hon. members realize that practically all the ore needed to make the
3,000,000 tons produced in Canada comes from the United States? The steel plants in Nova Scotia bring in ore from Brazil or Newfoundland, but the great steel plants in Ontario get their ore from the lake Superior region, from the Mesaba range. I was surprised to read the other day that there is only visible a ten years' supply in the open pits of the Mesaba range, and which furnish eighty-five per cent of the iron ore used in the United States and practically all that used by the steel plants in Ontario. There are other supplies of ore in the Mesaba range but they will have to go deeper for it, perhaps go into the mining of iron ore.
There is, however, plenty of iron ore in Canada. I am not particularly familiar with the iron ore deposits in the eastern provinces, but I have made some little study of those in British Columbia. I say without fear of successful contradiction that the iron ores of British Columbia contain a higher iron content than any other ore in the world. The Mesaba range ores contain only as high as fifty-one per cent iron, but those of British Columbia run as high as seventy per cent iron content. These ores are also low in the impurities, especially phosphorus and sulphur which are usually found in iron ore. There is also in British Columbia an abundance of coal and limestone. Over the years some forty-eight engineers have reported on more than thirty-two properties containing iron ore. All these properties are on tidewater. The question then arises: Why is it that no development has taken place in British Columbia or that no practical effort has been made to develop the iron ores of that province, as well as to do more in the way of developing the iron ores in other parts of Canada?
The fight which British Columbia has put up for the manufacture of steel in that province has been one of thirty years or more duration. It is most interesting to note that last year a special committee was set up by the United States senate, called the Truman committee. Sworn evidence was given before this committee that the Morgan-United States Steel corporation interests were behind the blocking of any move to develop steel production in British Columbia.

War Appropriation-Supplies

We have always suspected that the hands of Morgan and the United States Steel corporation were behind this, but here we, for the first time, have sworn testimony. It is interesting to note that the United States Steel corporation and the Morgan interests were present at that committee but as yet no rebuttal has been made to the sworn statements of Mr. Landahl of Seattle.
It may be asked why I am bringing up the question of steel production at this time. I do it for two reasons. First, I want to direct the attention of the minister and the committee to the reasons why the efforts put forth by the people of British Columbia and the western states have been thwarted. Second, there is a principle at stake. We have been living and are still living in the days of cartels and combines. To my mind this matter is so serious that I deem it my duty as a member to get up in my place this afternoon and ask that note be made of the statements made before the United States senate committee in August, 1942. Those statements were most damaging and should receive some consideration and investigation by the government of this country. I am not going to deal with all the proposals which have been put forward by British Columbia since the war began in connection with the erection of an electric furnace to melt our surplus steel scrap. We were promised that this would be done, and at one time actually thought it was to be an accomplished fact. The promise has recently been made by the minister that he will help to further this project, so that I shall not refer to the matter other than to say that it is rather strange that when the announcement appeared in the press two weeks ago that certain public-spirited men of Vancouver were coming to Ottawa to place the matter before the Minister of Munitions and Supply, the agent of the Morgan-United States Steel corporation interests was in the city and the chief agent of the corporation in Vancouver also appeared in Ottawa. That may have been only a coincidence, but to me it was a most remarkable coincidence. I may be a little suspicious, but I do not think they were here for their health. They were here, I believe, to watch and to continue blocking if they could any effort toward the establishment of a steel-making industry in British Columbia.
I have not the time this afternoon to read all the evidence given before the Truman committee, but I would advise hon. members to get a copy of this evidence and read it carefully, particularly the statements given

under oath about the iron ores of British Columbia. They will find in this evidence details of the fight that has gone on over a twenty-five year period. However, I should like to read one letter which I think will explain quite briefly some of the evidence which had been submitted. This is from Senator Thomas Voyce to Senator Lewis Schwellenbaeh, and it reads:
Dear Senator: I regret it was impossible to arrange a meeting between you and the men here who have charge of efforts to build a blast furnace on the Pacific coast.
The next best I can do is to write you and try to give you a view of this particular situation and bring about the action necessary, to place our situation before the President in Washington; he is in my judgment the only one able to assist the Pacific coast.
I enclose a memorandum giving a few details of the proposed industrial development.
When you read the memorandum and report enclosed, you will say-"if that is correct, why has no blast furnace been built on the Pacific coast" and that was what I was so anxious to go over with you.
I wanted you to know that since 1912 the Morgan-U.S. Steel Corporation groups have held the entire Pacific coast under control, ruining those that attempted to build a blast furnace on the Pacific coast, reaching into every source, issuing government pamphlets covering iron ores, coking coals, et cetera, stopping publishing favouring such, stopping newspapers from mentioning this development a second time, doing everything that power-frenzied men with unlimited cash generally do-first under the leadership of Judge Gary, and since his death merely as ordinary routine.
Instead of sending an ordinary engineer, it would be best to send a G man engineer; only one such could cope with the machinations of the Morgan-U.S. Steel Corporation groups, that are constantly in operation to prevent us on the Pacific coast from making use of our iron ores, coals, et cetera.
That is a very important letter because it deals not only with the iron ores of the western districts of the United States but with the iron ores of British Columbia which it was intended to use when a steel smelting plant could be developed in Washington, Oregon or California.
I also want to put on record a further statement. This is by Mr. Landahl, who appeared before that committee:
Every time an M.P. or someone of importance starts to press for iron and steel production in British Columbia, the local fifth column says -"let us have an (another) examination of our iron ore resources."
I want to point out here that again and again we have had examinations and reports on orr iron ores, one conflicting with the other and these conflicting reports have to

War Appropriation-Supplies
quite an extent been engendered by those opposed to the establishment of a steel plant on the Pacific coast. I continue the quotation:
For forty-three years there have been almost annual "examinations of the iron ore resources of the province of British Columbia." Numerous reports have been expensively printed by the governments.
Then he gives the names of the engineers who have made these reports and goes on to say:
Forty-eight mining engineers of fine repute, most of them, over one every year for forty-three years, and nobody stops this dreadful betrayal of the people.
Beginning of the year 1941, owing to the war, an agitation was on for starting pig iron production and the dominion and B.C. governments were moved to "have an (another) examination of our resources." Arthur G. McKee and Co. of Cleveland was engaged-did the -work

handed in report August 20, 1941. The report is marked as printed in 1941.
Copies of this report can now be obtained, but for some considerable time the report was prevented from being printed. I continue the quotation:
Latter part of May I was east and met an engineer that had been in B.C. when the McKee examination was under way. He showed me the report. I went through the same and asked-
Q. Where did you get all these wrong figures from?
A. From Doctor Walker and Mr. Wilkinson.
By the way, Mr. Wilkinson is agent in Vancouver for the United States Steel corporation. The quotation continues:
Q. Wilkinson, who is he?
A. He owns the Morrison Nail Works.
Q. Who took the McKee Company to Wilkinson?
A. Doctor Walker did (Walker is Deputy Minister of Mines).
Wilkinson is the mainland agent for the U.S.S. Corporation-He led the fight against the British Ironmasters in 1922-26.
While we avoided the Morgan-U.S. Steel Corporation, their emissaries ambushed us in every quarter and stopped every source we negotiated with from carrying out their undertakings. Briefly we found that-
(a)	They controlled all private finance in the United States.
(b)	They could influence in their favour all other finance, governmental and private, here and all other countries.
(c)	Only one man in the world ever successfully challenged their supremacy, and that was President Franklin D. Roosevelt.
When the matter was drawn to the President's attention last fall he obtained permission for the erection of a steel plant on the Pacific coast. And where do you think, Mr. Chairman, that steel plant is being built? Away down in the orange groves of California, where the steel interests realize that it must,
from its very location, disappear after this war is over. But at least President Franklin D. Roosevelt got action.
To my mind, Mr. Chairman, this matter is extremely serious. I know that the minister may tell us that man-power is short or that he is getting enough steel from the United States and Canada to fill the requirements, but there is no doubt, and I say this without fear of successful contradiction, that if the government had heeded the advice of the members from British Columbia in 1939 and 1940 that steel plant would have been in operation to-day in British Columbia and would certainly have been a great contributing factor in the building of more ships in Canada and in making available more steel.
I do not know whether I am right in saying this or not. But I feel it is pertinent to say at this time that even when the matter was put up by members of parliament from British Columbia in Ottawa last fall they were told by Mr. Kilbourn, the steel controller, that British Columbia did not have the ghost of a chance for a steel plant-did not have the ghost of a chance. So we found it all along the way. Every time we put up the proposition our efforts were thwarted. We were told that steel could be got elsewhere more cheaply than in British Columbia, and that after the war there would be an over-supply of steel. But, Mr. Chairman, the whole Pacific coast market is open there. During this war we have been transporting steel scrap from British Columbia across to the east at a cost of $15 per ton for freight and then bringing it back to British Columbia at $25 per ton freight, and in the face of the fact that British Columbia has an abundance of iron ores, ores with the highest iron content anywhere in the world, and has likewise available ample supplies of coal, and mountains of lime, all of which are on the seaboard.
I pointed out when I started, Mr. Chairman, that I had two objects in view. One was to bring this serious matter to the attention of the house and of the minister, and the other was to endeavour if I could in my small way to help break down the opposition outside this house who up to the present time have been able to thwart the people of British Columbia in developing its natural resources and in developing industries within that province. There is a principle at stake. While I know that it has been attempted unsuccessfully by other corporations, it is my opinion that if this steel cartel could be broken down so that we in British Columbia would be allowed to develop our iron ores, it might be the means of helping us also to break down
3610
War Appropriation-Supplies

other cartels which have been thwarting our advancement, and this must be done if we in British Columbia are to continue our onward march of progress in that province.
I might mention a serious matter that came to my attention the other day, which has to do with cartels but perhaps has nothing directly to do with steel. A canning manufacturer in New Westminster, who has built up a wonderful business, was approached some weeks ago by certain interests who wanted to buy that business. He told them it was not for sale. They offered him a wonderful price and he said, "No; it is my life's work, an industry I have built up by my own initiative." He was told by these men who approached him, "All right; keep it, but if we can we will put you out of business." That is extremely serious.
Mr. HOWE; That is a very serious charge, and the hon. member must give full particulars, the names of all parties, so that steps can be taken.
Mr. REID; I will tell the minister what I will do, to be fair. I will give him the names in confidence.
Not in confidence; give me the names.
I will give the minister the name of the man who was approached.
And the name of the man who approached him, I think.

I will try to find that out. I did not hear the name of the man who approached him, but I was very much impressed by the statement because it did not come from an irresponsible person, and I brought it in here to show that there are certain interests in this country who are determined that certain provinces, either east or west, will not progress or have certain industries. As the minister knows, I have stood in my place, as was my duty, and pointed out the danger of centralization of industries in the country. It is not the easiest thing to stand against the government or the minister, and I am not blaming the minister for this matter of steel because it has been going on for thirty or thirty-five years. But he has men outside in his department who are not giving him right advice, or if they are giving him advice it is negative: do not allow British Columbia to develop; they do not need it.
I felt I was carrying out the trust given me by the people of New Westminster in rising in my place and in my humble way bringing 'the matter to the attention of the minister and of the house in the hope that it might do (Mr. Reid.]
some good in helping to break down, if possible, these outside of governments themselves who up to the present time have controlled' to quite an extent the industrial life of this and other countries.

I am sure that hon. members will forgive me if I do not follow their arguments through. I have listened with interest to the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). I read the United States evidence to which he referred, and I heard the evidence given here last autumn. I believe he was thoroughly justified in bringing before the committee the question of the manufacture of steel on the Pacific coast of Canada.
The statement which the minister made on Friday was of an extremely creditable achievement. I think the whole house will agree with that assertion. It indicates what industrial planning, even when it is taken, if I may say so, rather unwillingly and under pressure, can do for a nation. Of the various phases of the minister's statement, members of our party in this house will have something to say subsequently. Taken as a whole, the record indicates what this country can do when it has a well-defined purpose in view.
And leadership.

Substantial advances on purchase contracts of critical and strategic materials have been made to China and Russia, and in connection with purchases in some Latin-American countries.
May 13, 1941, OPM requested that the initial contract be doubled. This was concluded at the same price. The company ashed for an advance of $25,000,000 against this contract, and a loan for this amount was made to it by the Export-Import Bank at three per cent interest.
In negotiating contracts with the Aluminum Company of America to build and operate aluminum plants in the United States for our account, we secured a reduction from Alcoa-
The Aluminum Company of America.
-in the price of aluminum in the United States from 17 cents to 15 cents per pound, thereby saving the government a great many millions of dollars.
I want to draw attention particularly to this paragraph:
After getting the reduced price from Alcoa, we asked the Aluminum Company of Canada to reduce their price from 17 cents to 15 cents, notwithstanding we had contracted to pay 17 cents. The company was reluctant to reduce the price since they were getting 17 cents from the British and Canadian governments. However, we finally prevailed upon them to reduce the price to 15 cents on 80 per cent of the shipments. To get this reduction in price, we waived the interest on the advances, and made a reduction in the amortization requirements. The reduction from 17 cents to 15 cents saved Metals Reserve Company $16,000,000, while only $2,500.000 was waived in interest. This revision of the previous contracts provided for an increase in our purchases of aluminum from Canada to
