speechtext: Is that a copy?

It is a copy. But the contents of the letter have been cheeked. When I returned to Ottawa and read again the minister's speech made on March 23,
[Mr. Coldwell.l
I thought perhaps I or the stenographer who copied the letter had made a mistake in the date, and consequently 1 telegraphed Washington to have a check made of the date of the letter. I received this reply:
Re your telegram this morning offices Jesse Jones and Senator Truman both confirm March 24 1943 date on Jones letter.

May I interrupt for a
minute? That letter is not inconsistent with what I said in the house. I was not aware of the arrangement with the Jesse Jones agency-the Metals Reserve Company, I believe it is called-because it did not pass through the Department of Munitions and Supply. It was a contract between the Metals Reserve Company and the Aluminum Company of Canada Limited. The first intimation I had of it was an intimation from a United States source that a price of 15 cents has been contracted for with the United States agency. I immediately advised the Aluminum Company of Canada that the price to Canada and the price to Great Britain would also be 15 cents, and that was accepted and the contracts were revised accordingly. The fact that the Metals Reserve corporation did not make a price of 15 cents for their total purchase is news to me. But what I intended to say was that existing contracts between the Aluminum Company of Canada and Britain-in the meantime the British government had appointed me their agent to deal with aluminum matters-were revised on a 15 cents basis converted into Canadian funds.

Well, it will be noted that the Aluminum Company of Canada was reluctant to reduce the price from 17 to 15 cents to the United States government because they were getting 17 cents from the British and Canadian governments.

Yes; but may I say that
there is a vast difference in the relative positions. The new plants in the United States were built with funds furnished by the United States government and are owned by that government, whereas the Aluminum Company of Canada were making metal in plants which they themselves owned.

I shall have something to say about that in a few minutes, but I would draw the minister's attention to this, that 15 cents and 17 cents a pound were the exact prices originally agreed upon among members of the international cartel which was formed in 1931. That is the cartel known as Alliance Limited, a cartel which, by the way, included Farbenindustrie of Germany

War Appropriation-Supplies
until 1942. Indeed, as far as the parent company of Aluminum of Canada is concerned, namely, Aluminium Limited, so far as I know it has not been dissolved; that is, the cartel of which Farbenindustrie was a part.
On May 14 I also drew attention to the fact that the prospectus of the company referred to what was termed a reduction in the base selling price of aluminum, and I noticed that the minister used the same words in March.
I concluded that there must be some provision for some price other than the base price. I understand that some four contracts were made between the Metals Reserve Corporation and the Aluminum Company of Canada, and of course these contracts have been referred to on the floor of congress; references will be found at page 1943 of the congressional appendix, by Hon. John M. Coffee. I understand that these contracts contain what is known in the United States, and sometimes in Canada too, as an escalator clause, which provides that in the event of certain costs, including wages, raw material, transportation or insurance increasing, the price shall be advanced proportionately and accordingly. So that there is another price than the one mentioned in the contract. In other words, the price referred to in the prospectus as the base price of fifteen cents or seventeen cents, as the case may be, is only a base price, the actual price may be higher. Whether even the minimum price of fifteen cents is fair and reasonable is a matter to which I wish to draw the attention of this committee.
In the meantime I am going to ask the minister to tell the committee, when he has something to say, what are the actual prices per pound we have paid and are paying for aluminum, now and since the outbreak of the war. In the course of an investigation into the operations of the Aluminum Company of America, and in a brief submitted to the courts on behalf of the United States government, references are made to the cost of producing commercial ingots at Arvida in the year 1937. Not only will you find the reference there; it will be found also in the annual report of the company for 1937 or 1938, when Mr. E. K. Davis, president of Aluminium Limited, made the statement that they were selling some aluminum at thirteen cents a pound and that this gave Aluminum of Canada a profit of four cents a pound, giving a cost at that time, estimated in that way, of nine cents a pound; and it was admitted by the company before the United States courts that in that year, with a relatively small production, with the equipment then installed and including in the price the profits made by the
subsidiary companies in the production of bauxite, power and so forth, the Arvida plant was producing commercial ingots at a price of 8-93 cents a pound. To-day the new aluminum plant, with the latest, most modern and most efficient machinery, producing, as the minister told us on Friday, six times as much aluminum as in 1939, still charges fifteen cents and seventeen cents a pound as a base price.
That is a profit of 100 per cent.

With the vastly increased production and the more modern equipment, Aluminium Limited at its subsidiary's Arvida plant should produce the metal at a much lower figure than in 1937. Let me repeat that the prices set by the corporation and agreed to by the government are the prices set in 1931 by the international cartel, Alliance Limited. Again let me remark that if the sister company, the Aluminum Company of America, with higher labour costs and more expensive power, can produce the metal and maintain its very high profits, as it has done and is doing, on the basis of fifteen cents a pound, then obviously the Aluminum Company of Canada is able to produce and sell aluminum to the Canadian, United States, Australian and other united nations governments at a price considerably less than that at which the United States company can sell to the government of that country.
I say the united nations are being sold down the Saguenay river by these agreements; that while our people are called upon to sacrifice, and while Canadian boys are giving their lives in a great cause, this giant corporation is receiving profits and properties which will enable it after the war to maintain a monopoly which will dominate electric power resources and the production of aluminum on the American continent and to a large extent throughout the world. This is a serious condition, and I intend to prove these statements this afternoon, if I have time.
To understand the effect of the government's policy in regard to the aluminum companies it is necessary to delve into their history and to trace, as briefly as possible, the steps by which they have secured their stranglehold both on aluminum and on the nations. I shall take the Aluminum Company of America first, because it was originally the parent of all the companies affiliated with Aluminium Limited. It can be shown that this has been a highly profitable monopoly for many years. An analysis of the financial history of this corporation reveals the enormous profits made by the owners. In 1905 the original capital, including not only cash but
War Appropriation-Supplies

stock issued in payment for patents, amounted to not more than $3,121,600. Thirty years later, in 1935, the original investment, without the investment of another cent raised from themselves or from the public, gave the owners assets in Alcoa and its creature, Aluminium Limited, totalling $167,500,000. By 1942 those assets had jumped to over $350,000,000 for Aluminium Limited alone. In the twenty-five years from 1911 to 1935 the profits available for securities representing the original investment of $3,121,600 totalled $240,000,000, indicating an annual return of 282 per cent. Out of this some $81,274,000 was paid in cash dividends, representing a cash return of 100 per cent per year paid on the original investment. Imagine what will be the vast increase in the assets of the corporation as a result of the accelerated depreciation now being granted by Canada 1 This enormous accumulation of wealth, representing mainly gains derived from monopoly power and privileged access to valuable hydro-electric resources, has been concentrated in the hands of a mere handful of people. There has been no wide diffusion of ownership of aluminum shares, some ninety per cent of the stock being held by directors and members of their families.
It is to this company that the governments of Canada, the United States, Great Britain and Australia are giving millions of dollars over and above the real value of the aluminum during the course of the present war. That is what the agreements really do.
The lifelong policy of the aluminum corporation has been to maintain high prices for its product, the effect of which has been to restrict its use. General Motors, for example, abandoned its use years ago on account of Alcoa's arbitrary price-fixing policy. The Ford Motor Company about the same time turned to steel in order to escape the monopoly stranglehold. Other companies followed the same path. On the eve of the expiration of its original patents, in 1906 and 1909, it entered upon a plan to secure control of raw materials which might be used by any possible competitor. It secured agreements with three of its most profitable competitors not to supply bauxite to other producers or manufacture aluminum for periods of forty and fifty years. It undertook to tie up the principal waterpower companies in North America so that no competitor could obtain electric power for the manufacture of aluminum. This it succeeded in doing.
For example, on August 14, 1899, Alcoa entered into a contract with the Shawinigan Water and Power Company of Shawinigan Falls, Quebec, Canada, for the supply of 
power. Like its other contracts for power, this contract contained a restrictive covenant by which the power company agreed that it would not use its power for the manufacture of aluminum, or sell power to any manufacturer of aluminum other than Alcoa. Section 12 of the contract provided:
In consideration of t, e agreement by Aluminum Company of America that the power generated by the water privileges granted by this contract shall be used for tile purpose of the manufacture of aluminum and such purposes as may be incidental thereto, and for lighting and heating the premises of said second party and for no other purposes, the Shawinigan Water and Power Company of Shawinigan Falls, Quebec, Canada, agrees that it will not furnish water or water-power to any other person, corporation or organization engaged in the business of manufacturing aluminum and further that said Shawinigan Water and Power Company itself will not use water or waterpower for or in connection with the business of manufacturing aluminum during the continuance of this contract, or of any renewal thereof, it being the true intent and meaning hereof that with respect to the manufacture of aluminum the rights to be granted and conveyed unto the Aluminum Company of America shall be sole and exclusive.
Section 16 of the contract gave to this restrictive covenant the status of a covenant running with the land of the power company. The contract was to continue for a period of ten years, subject to successive renewals for periods of ten years. Subsequent contracts renewed this covenant, and it is still in effect. Contracts of exactly similar sort were made with Niagara and other power corporations, so that eventually Alcoa controlled power everywhere along the St. Lawrence in Canada and the United States. One might properly remark that Canada's Combines Investigation Act is a dead letter, so far as these giant monopolies are concerned.
As early as 1896 Alcoa entered into an agreement with its only competitor, a Swiss company, to divide the world markets between them. But by 1901 French and British companies had made their appearance so that it became necessary to enlarge the cartel. In order to get around the United States Sherman anti-trust law, the Alcoa formed a Canadian subsidiary, the Northern Aluminum Company, and from that day to this it has endeavoured to circumvent United States laws with respect to trusts and cartels by using Canadian corporations.
From 1919 to 1925, George D. Haskell, president of the Baush Machine Tool company, endeavoured to find ways and means of manufacturing his own aluminum. He got in touch with James B. Duke, the owner of the power plant and water power on the Saguenay river. As soon as Arthur Vining Davis, the president and financial genius of
[DOT] .

War Appropriation-Supplies
the Aluminum Company of America, heard of it, he saw Duke and negotiated a merger with him whereby Duke became a partner and one of seven directors with the ownership of fifteen per cent of the common stock and one-ninth of the preferred stock. Duke had paid $1,000,000 for the Saguenay power sites which the province of Quebec had alienated for $40,000. The market value of the stock which Duke received for the Shipshaw or lower Saguenay site was approximately $40,000,000. He retained the upper site which Duke-Price Power had already developed.
Duke died in 1925, and in 1926 Alcoa acquired 53i per cent control of the Duke-Price Power Company which owned the upper development and immediately entered into a fifty year contract with it to take 100,000 horse-power at a total cost of $60,000,000.
By these measures all contemplated competition was eliminated.
I do not propose to go into the methods by which bauxite deposits were acquired in the United States, British Guiana, Dutch Guiana and elsewhere. Suffice it to say that similar, methods were followed, and successfully.
An interesting sidelight of the character of the economic barons into whose hands the government's policies are delivering Canada, is shown by the manner in which they succeeded in obtaining a large block of shares willed by Charles M. Hall, the inventor of the process, to the American Missionary Society. Within a few months of acquiring the stock from the beneficiaries at $5 a share, it was selling at $79 a share. The earnings on this stock that year, 1925, was $13.22 a share. Davis acquired over
61.000	of these shares for himself, and some
49.000	of them went to Duke in part payment of the power site.
Meantime in 1924 the Northern Aluminum Company, the subsidiary of the Aluminum Company of America, had become known as the Aluminum Company of Canada. Its business had expanded into the making of aluminum wire and sheet and it owned bauxite deposits in British Guiana. With the acquisition of the Duke-Price Power Company it changed the name of the Duke-Price Power to the Saguenay Power Company Limited and entered, as I have said, into the fifty-year contract to take power at a total cost of $60,000,000. This contract was guaranteed by Alcoa.
Now the stage was all set for the creation of a world cartel into which Alcoa could not enter on account of the United States antitrust laws. It remembered that in 1912 the United States Department of Justice had ordered the dissolution of the agreement with
the Swiss company. But it also remembered that through its subsidiary, the _ Northern Aluminum Company, it had entered into agreements designed to control sales outside the United States. As a result it succeeded at once, in 1912, in raising the price of aluminum in the United States from 17 cents a pound to 26-46 cents a pound. After the world war it entered into various informal agreements and understandings to restrict competition and maintain high prices. As can be established from the records, between 1921 and 1927, it supplemented these agreements by acquiring producing facilities in the home markets of foreign producers, notably Norwegian.
In 1928, the directors of Aluminum Company of America decided that they were sufficiently strong to dominate the world. Because the Sherman anti-trust law made their own entry into a world cartel dangerous, they decided to form a new company under Canadian law. Thus they created Aluminium Limited and at once transferred to it thirty-three of its foreign subsidiaries, including the Aluminum Company of Canada. How closely these companies remain one is shown by the ownership of stock in them. The latest report I have been able to secure, that of 1938, shows that 81 per cent of Alcoa stock is held by the ' people who also hold 83-93 per cent of the stock of Aluminium Limited which now became the parent company of the Aluminum Company of Canada, which it owns fully, and thirty-two other companies outside the United States. It is of the parent company, Aluminium Limited, that our minister at Washington, Mr. Leighton McCarthy, is a vice-president and director at the present time.
No.
Yes, excuse me.
Not at the present time.
Unless he has resigned in the last three weeks.
He resigned last February.

That was from the
Aluminum Company of Canada. I asked Mr. McCarthy when I was in Washington three weeks ago the direct question as to whether or not it was true that he was a vice-president and director of the parent company, which I had miscalled the Aluminum Company of the United States, but which I should have called Aluminium Limited, and Mr. McCarthy's reply was this: "Yes, I am a director of Aluminium Limited, and I am intending to remain a director of that company."

And vice-president.
War Appropria tion-Supplies
To what agreement does my hon. friend refer?

The general agreement with the Aluminum Company for the expansion of their plant, for increasing their electric power, the agreements regarding depreciation allowance, the price of aluminum-the several agreements.
To argue that because Sir Stafford Cripps or someone else expressed appreciation of the
War Appropria tion-Supplies

quality and quantity of their product, the contracts and agreements are sound is to deceive oneself and the country. I have no doubt their product is good. I have no doubt the quantity is satisfactory. I have no doubt that the material is vital, but I am not overlooking the fact that they dictated their own terms. Look again at the letter written by Mr. Jesse Jones on March 24 last.
What year?

This year, 1943. He says:
We asked the Aluminum Company of Canada to reduce their price from 17 cents to 15 cents, notwithstanding we had contracted to pay 17 cents. The company was reluctant to reduce the price since they were getting 17 cents from the British and Canadian governments.
Nothing in this to merit any thanks from Britain or from Canada. -On the contrary, it seems clear they were out to get all the traffic would bear, while Canadian boys died across the seas and our people at home worked and saved to prosecute the war.
But there is another and, in the long run, a more serious aspect to this situation. I have shown, I think conclusively, that we are dealing with a group of industrial barons whose chief aim has been to make money and obtain world-wide power. Yet it is to this organization the several governments have given, or advanced, over $300,000,000 in one form or another during this war. It is easily the greatest financial grab ever pulled off in the history of Canada.
Cost-free new aluminum facilities, and the power plant at Shipshaw will do two things: (1) enable them to control more effectively than ever the light metal industry of the world and (2) undersell publicly-owned power in the northeastern part of North America.
I have shown the interest of the Aluminum companies in electric power at various stages of their development. From the evidence, there can be no doubt whatsoever that the effective control of power and power development was a weapon used to prevent the establishment of rival companies. Thus their complete control and war-time development of the whole of the power resources of the Saguenay river are ominous from that point of view.
In spite of various attempts on the part of the Hydro Electric Commission of Ontario to obtain international agreements for the development of the St. Lawrence, nothing has been done. The dominant interest in the St. Lawrence area has been and is-including Beauhamois-the Aluminum Company, whose agents have endeavoured at all times to
l Mr. Coldwell.]
block public power development on the river. But this phase will be dealt with by one of my colleagues.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has spoken for fifty minutes.

I should like to finish if I may, Mr. Chairman.
Some hon. MEAIBERS: Go ahead.

I do not propose now to deal with the labour aspects of this company's activities. They can be dealt with at another time. Suffice it to say, such relations have often been both scandalous and inhuman. Alen in the pot room rarely last long amid the poisonous fumes, and the labour turnover in that part of the plant is appalling. Cheap labour, cheap power and high monopoly prices for their product have brought the Aluminum interests untold wealth and economic power.
Now I think I have proved what I intended to prove:
1.	That the price we are paying for aluminum is a monopoly price,, substantially set by the world cartel in 1931, and out of line with the actual cost of production.
2.	That the information given to this house on March 23 was not in accordance with the true facts, because, as the minister now points out, he did not know what the facts were.
3.	The minister also denied that the $68,500,000 was an advance, a balance of which might be cancelled and the Aluminum Company thereby relieved of the balance.
Air. HOW'E: I did not say it was not advanced but it was not for the Shipshaw development. It was advanced to build pot rooms for making the aluminum.
The minister will find that he said that it could not be cancelled.
The cost of the pot rooms cannot be cancelled. The other can.
I was going to draw attention to the letter of Mr. Jones in which he says that the contracts make provision for a fixed basis of cancellation.
Is it Jesse Jones or Jesse James?

Jesse Jones. To go on with my point:
4.	The minister stated that all aluminum produced in Canada is sold at the same price whoever buys it. Mr. Jones' letter states that.

War Appropriation-Supplies
there are two base prices, fifteen and seventeen cents. I would ask the minister to tell us the prices actually paid.
5.	The electric power development, which was paid for by the government in large measure, in fact wholly if you take the deal as a whole, menaces the future of publicly-owned hydro electric enterprise.
I am asking if the minister will table all the contracts made with the company on behalf of the Canadian, British, Australian and United States governments so that we may see what is in them.
I have placed the facts before the committee without invective, I am certain without exaggeration, and I know without misrepresentation. These are the facts as I have accumulated them. I have got them first hand from first-hand sources. I have no doubt that there are certain people who know the people I visited when I was in Washington and know the offices where I got my information. I assure the committee that my information is authentic and gathered from those who were able to give me the information. I ask, is there an hon. member who will dare now to rise in his place and say that the deal with this giant unit of an international cartel is not, without exaggeration, a grave danger to the country and a public scandal?
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
speechtext:
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) made certain remarks about the aluminum contracts, for which he suggests the department has been responsible. I wish to say just a few words in that regard, and I will give the facts asked for at a later sitting.
I think we will all agree with regard to the importance of aluminum in this war. We know that, at the time the first contract was being made, the women of Britain were delivering up their pots and pans, in order that aeroplanes might be manufactured to save the battle of Britain. I am happy to say that Canada was able to make a very substantial contribution of aluminum at that time. Had we not been able to do so, I think it is possible that the battle of Britain, instead of being won, might have been lost. We know the importance of aluminum to-day.
Without aluminum the manufacture of combat aircraft is impossible. We know that Canada's tremendous contribution of aluminum has made possible the great expansion in the production of aeroplanes, not only in Britain and in the United States, but in this country as well. That I think has been of very great importance to the war effort, and therefore no one in this chamber will disagree with me when I say that Canada was in duty bound to provide all the aluminum it could, and to take every step that could be taken to that end.
With that premise, we can examine the aluminum contracts. Let me say that the Department of Munitions and Supply has been fighting one battle and one battle only, namely, the battle against the axis. It has not been fighting a battle against trusts and combines. It has not been fighting a battle for one industry as against another, or for one province as against another. It has been trying to mobilize the industrial resources of Canada for the most effective battle against the axis.	_	_ _
We have heard in great deail that Aluminium Limited, the parent company of the Aluminum Company of Canada, is a combine. I daresay that is true. It has been a combine^ for a great many years, and I presume it is a combine to-day. But whether it is a combine or not, the government has not had time to take up a war against any combine, even though it were inclined to do so. As I say, we have been fighting one war, namely the war against the axis, and we have mobilized Canadian industry, as it was at the outbreak of war, for the purpose of fighting the axis. As a matter of fact, we have tried not to use the excuse of the war for changing the competitive position of any industry in Canada. Every industry has been treated exactly the same as any other. If any industry has come to the Department of Munitions and Supply and said, "We are capable of producing more of any article required for war than we are doing at present; these are our plans for doing so," we have examined the proposal very carefully, and if it could be fitted into the pattern being followed by the department for expansion we have encouraged that industry to expand.
We have done that for every industry. We have not singled out a few industries and said, "We will expand you, but your competitor will have to stay as he is." Any industry that has had the desire and the ambition and courage to expand to meet war needs has been encouraged to do so by my department, and perhaps financially assisted to do so.

War Appropriation-Supplies
May I remind the minister that there is no competitor in this case?
Quite so, and there never was a competitor as far as Canada is concerned.
If you had not this aluminum, what would be the result in the production of equipment?

There would be no aeroplanes, or fewer aeroplanes. As to the dealings of the Department of Munitions and Supply, it has been pointed out that Alcoa, the Aluminum Company of America, was the original company on this continent manufacturing aluminum. It has been pointed out that the Aluminum Company of Canada was organized as part of the Aluminum Company of America. It has also been pointed out that at a certain stage in the development of the aluminum company, the parent company was established in Canada, and that the Aluminum Company of Canada and certain foreign companies manufacturing aluminum were combined under the aegis of Aluminium Limited. There is no question about that.
I might point out that in farming Aluminium Limited as a Canadian company, subject to Canadian laws, and transferring the Canadian holdings of Alcoa to Canada and placing that company under Canadian law, a step in advance was taken as far as Canada is concerned. I think we will agree that any company that is Canadian, subject to Canadian law, is a better citizen of Canada than a company "which is merely a branch of a United States company; obviously a company having its head office in another country is not subject to Canadian law to the same extent. However, I may say that so far as I could follow the remarks of the hon. member before the dinner recess, he was quoting from evidence produced by Thurman Arnold in his investigation of the Aluminum Company of America.
Thurman Arnold of course had a great reputation as a trust-buster or of a breaker of combines. Mr. Arnold, as special prosecutor for the government of the United States, conducted a case against the Aluminum Company of America which was in the courts of the United States for more than three years. I am sorry I have ndt refreshed my memory about the details of the prosecution, but I recall that over 300 charges were brought against the Aluminum Company of America. After an exhaustive inquiry which covered three years, and reams of evidence, the court gave its decision, finding the Aluminum Company of America not guilty on every charge laid by the United States government. So 
much for the charge that the Aluminum company is a trust and in combine illegally with the aluminum companies throughout the world. I simply state that for what it is worth, but once again I say that the Department of Munitions and Supply has not been conducting a war against combines. It has taken industry as it found it, has tried to get the greatest production possible out of industry, and its purpose is to leave industry in exactly the same competitive position as at the outbreak of war. After the war, under normal conditions, if any government desires to proceed against Aluminium Limited, or against Aluminum Company of Canada as a combine, that will be perfectly in order, but I think every hon. member will agree with me, that we should not use the excuse of war to do something that we cannot appropriately do in peace time, as far as attacking the competitive position of any industry in Canada is concerned.
As to the purchase of aluminum, the first transactions between Britain and the Aluminum Company of Canada were carried out without Canadian intervention. The Ministry of Aircraft Production had, and still has, a representative in the United States. It was that representative of the Minister of Aircraft Production who conducted the negotiations with the Aluminum Company of Canada which led to the first British contract. The United States contracts were worked out by the Metals Reserve Corporation, or whatever is the appropriate agency of the United States government, direct with the aluminum company. I have never seen the United States contracts and have not a copy of them. It was news to me that those contracts mentioned two prices. I know that the price change in the United States took place while the contracts were under negotiation. When the first United States contract was drawn, the price of aluminum in the United States was seventeen cents a pound, and the first contract between the United States and the Aluminum Company of Canada mentioned a price of seventeen cents a pound. While a second contract was being negotiated the price of aluminum was revised in the United States, owing I think largely to the fact that the United States government had paid for the building of plants which manufacture aluminum in that country, and had demanded a reduction in price on that account. In any event, at that stage the base price in the United States was reduced to fifteen cents. By that time I had been appointed the agent of the British government in its aluminum transactions. I immediately demanded a reduction in the price of aluminum to Canada and to Britain, to correspond with

War Appropriation-Supplies
the reduction to the United States. That demand was granted, and prices were revised accordingly to Britain, Australia and Canada.
Canada, for her own purposes, has not required expanded facilities. We were entitled to the facilities which were in Canada when the war broke out, and to date we have not required more aluminum than those original facilities would provide. Therefore Canada has not contracted with the Aluminum Company of Canada for additional ingot capacity.
We have been told repeatedly that Canada has financed this expansion with its own funds. That is not true; we have provided no money whatever to the aluminum company for expansion.
Would the minister permit a question?
Yes.
What expansion has he in mind when he says "this expansion"?
Every expansion. Everything that the aluminum company has built in Canada since the war began.
I was just trying to gather what the minister meant. I understood him to say that they did not need to expand-

-to supply the Canadian
demand.
That there was already sufficient expansion?

They have expanded vastly,
of course, to supply the demand from the United States and from Britain.
We have provided a certain accelerated depreciation. I will divide that into two stages. One is the special depreciation for the expansion required to fill the United States order for aluminum. The United States order was placed with the knowledge that no facilities existed in Canada to fill the order, and that these facilities must be constructed, and constructed as part of the price of the aluminum which would go to the United States. The contract was drawn with the understanding that a loan would be made by the United States sufficient to pay for the pot rooms and other manufacturing facilities, needed to turn out the aluminum required by the United States within the time mentioned in the contract.
May I ask the minister a question?
Yes.
Was there any restriction in fact regarding that loan? It could be used for anything?

I think there were no restrictions placed on the use of that loan. That, of course, is a matter between the United States and the aluminum company; but the amount was the amount required to pay for the pot rooms, and alumina plants and all other facilities which are required to manufacture aluminum in ingot form.
That contract could have been written differently. It could have been written that the aluminum would be purchased for ten cents, and the equivalent of five cents could have been paid the aluminum company as capital to create the facilities which would manufacture aluminum. In that event there would have been the investment in Canada of so many dollars in capital facilities, which of course would not have 'been taxable, and there would have been the sale of aluminum to the United States at 10 cents a pound, the profits on which would have been taxable. Had the transaction been framed in that way there would have been no criticism whatever in this house. That type of investment in Canada has been going on for many years, and has been very welcome as a source of capital for industrial purposes in this country.

Does the minister feel
that there would have been profits at ten cents a pound?

I will cover that presently. You are all set to make a speech; let me continue mine. That would not have been as valuable a transaction for Canada as the present transaction. It probably would, indeed it must, have taken that form had we refused to allow accelerated depreciation on that part of the purchase price which went into fixed capital. The difference would have been this: Had the deal been organized in that way, the Aluminum Company of Canada would own an asset which they would have been allowed to depreciate over the'years; as it is, they own an asset which is fully depreciated. In other words, any dollar of earnings that comes from that asset is taxable as income by the Canadian government.
Let me point out to hon. gentlemen^ that, when anyone invests money in building a manufacturing plant or any other industrial enterprise, he has an obligation from the state that that capital will be returned to him over the years as depreciation. That is a very valuable concession granted him by the state. If you look over the balance sheets of industrial companies, you will find that each year
War Appropriation-Supplies

there is a deduction before taxation of perhaps five or six per cent of the original capital in the form of depreciation. Through accelerated depreciation, the new aluminum facilities will exhaust all rights to depreciation. That write-off can never occur in the future. Therefore, as I say, any earnings which will be made by the aluminum company from these facilities will be taxable in full. So that when we compare the deal which my hon. friend would say would be quite proper-that is, that five cents a pound would be paid by the United States as capital invested in Canada, and the aluminum sold at ten cents a pound- the position of Canada would have been vastly worse as far as taxable income is concerned than is the present situation.
We come now to Shipshaw. I noticed that my hon. friend did not make this mistake in his discussion this afternoon, but in the United States it has been stated definitely that the money which paid for the Shipshaw development was loaned to the aluminum company by the United States. As a matter of fact, the Shipshaw transaction was worked out well before the United States became a purchaser of aluminum in Canada. It was quite obvious that we would be very short of power for war purposes in the Quebec area. The Aluminum Company of Canada, as I have said before, had partly completed development at Shipshaw on which there had been spent some $35,000,000 and which was producing some 200,000 horsepower. Before the war it was estimated that the expenditure of another $35,000,000 or perhaps $38,000,000 would complete the development and provide a potential one million horsepower at that location.
Over a, period of time.

Well, as fast as it could be built. It is not finished yet; they are adding new turbines right along; but the dam was there; the construction was there for a million horsepower, and by May of next year the project will be producing a million horsepower. The potential horsepower was needed. It has been suggested that this development was carried out to block the St. Lawrence development. Let me remind hon. members that Canada is committed to the St. Lawrence development; that it has agreed with the United States to proceed with that development, and the St. Lawrence development was blocked not in Canada but in the United States. An exchange of notes took place which put us definitely on record as being willing and anxious to proceed with the St. Lawrence development. Had an agreement been completed, perhaps we would not have 
been anxious to proceed with Shipshaw; but not having the St. Lawrence development, we could not win the war with its help. We had to have a development that would give results, and therefore we encouraged the Shipshaw development. It has been suggested that we allowed an accelerated depreciation on the entire cost of the Shipshaw development. We did not; we allowed accelerated depreciation on sixty per cent of the cost.
I think I said that.

Perhaps so. That percentage was worked out very carefully. Construction costs were soaring at the time. The cost of turbines, which had to come largely from the United States, had more than doubled when the agreement was made. It was obvious that labour was becoming more difficult to obtain, and we were pressing the aluminum company to do the job in half the time they had intended to take when their estimate was made up. After going very carefully into all the factors and studying the question for months-we had engineers studying the possibilities-we decided that if we were to ask the aluminum company to carry out that expansion in war time, in a period of high prices, we were justified in reducing the charges on the plant to forty per cent of the cost, allowing the other sixty per cent to be written off by the company out of war-time profits. That transaction, as I say, was a Canadian transaction; the United States had nothing to do with it. The transaction had been concluded before the sale of aluminum to the United States took place, and the Shipshaw development should not be involved in any way with the transaction that has been under discussion here this afternoon and evening.
There was some other phase of my hon. friend's discussion with which I intended to deal. I will say this, that the Aluminum Company of Canada have carried out their contracts to the letter. They have delivered every pound of aluminum they have contracted to deliver, at the time for which the aluminum was promised. They have shown tremendous courage, taking on great liabilities, in carrying out the expansion that has been required by the united nations for their war programmes. It has been suggested here that the earning power of the aluminum company has been expanded enormously. If that is so, I suggest that it should be reflected in the market price of the shares of the company. Those shares now are exactly the same shares the company had outstanding before the war; they are bought and sold freely on the Montreal stock

War Appropriation-Supplies
exchange. Perhaps the fairest value of any security is its current quotation on the stock exchange.
What were they last year? They were 65.

True. What were they in 1939? They were 140. They are about 120 to-day, but before any war expansion took place they sold at 140 and kept around that level fairly consistently. Since the expansion has taken place, the shares have dropped steadily, until about a year ago. In recent months there has been buying that has brought them up to the present price which, as I say, is about 120. I had occasion to look up the price range; I am sorry I have not the figures here, but I would say simply that those who sell at 120 evidently think the company has less earning power to-day than it had in 1939, while those who buy at 120 probably think it is nearly as good as it was in 1939. But there is no class of buyer who seems to believe that these shares should be bought in large blocks at this time, at rising prices.
Therefore, in discussing the relations of the Department of Munitions and Supply with the Aluminum Company of Canada, I think I can say that the aluminum company have given value for anything that has been invested in this country by other governments. They have sold aluminum at the cheapest price at which it has been sold by any country. Incidentally I may say that the aluminum company in England is selling its aluminum at some seven or eight cents more than the price at which it is being sold in Montreal to-day. I think that is all I have to say at the moment; I shall look over Hansard and perhaps amplify my remarks to-morrow.
What is the actual price Canada is paying for aluminum?

The base price for aluminum to-day is fifteen cents, which may be increased or decreased according to increases or decreases in the cost of wages, transportation and power. The big item in which the cost has advanced is transportation. In the old days bauxite was brought in ships from British Guiana to Ha Ha bay on the Saguenay, and the cost of transportation was very low. To-day it is brought from British Guiana to an island in the Caribbean; there it is transhipped and brought to any United States port from New Orleans to New York. There it is transhipped by rail, and pays rail freight to the Saguenay. That, of course, has added enormously to the transportation costs.
Would the minister give the adjustment?

I can give the last adjustment. The last adjustment was about two cents over the base price. It is the same to all p0wers-to the United States, Canada and England. I will find the effect of the escalator clause in each of the years to which it has been adjusted. It is fixed by Price, Waterhouse and Company, who have been appointed referees for all buying countries, as to the actual differential between the base cost and the present day cost. I might say that the price of power has gone down, the price of wages has gone up slightly, and the price of transportation has gone up enormously.
When the minister said that later on he would give the facts asked for by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, did he mean he would table the contracts?
Certainly, such contracts as I have. I have not the first British contract, I never had it. I have not the United States contracts.
The minister will table the British contract?
I cannot do that; we are under agreement with the British government not to do so. I will table any Canadian contract I have.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) made an excellent speech in connection with the general productivity of industry under the supervision of the Minister of Munitions and Supply. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) gave the committee an informative address in relation to iron and steel production. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) delivered another informative address on the subject of aluminum, a subject concerning which the minister has spoken for the last half hour.
For the next half hour I shall speak on the subject of oil. Before commencing any detailed discussion I would point out to the minister that while in his opinion it is not the business of the government at the present time to take up questions in connection with combines, the United States government does. They have had exhaustive inquiries and investigations by senate committees into the supply of both rubber and oil. And from what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has said I presume they have had an exhaustive inquiry into the production of aluminum. I believe it is this government's business-any government's business-to see that the people are not exploited. I am not saying that they
War Appropriation-Supplies

are. I am going to wait until other arguments are offered along the lines of those given to-day. But I maintain it is the government's business, in spite of the war to prevent the exploitation of the Canadian people.
As I said on April 14, 1943, I was greatly depressed by the minister's speech on the subject of oil. I had built my hopes on the belief that the time was not far distant when Canada would be independent of any outside sources of oil, both economically and defensively; I had built up that belief in my mind from the exhaustive reports issued by the government's engineers. But I must confess I do not believe the minister-well, I will not say that I do not believe-rather, I have not been convinced that the minister himself is in favour of Canada's becoming independent, in the matter of oil production.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said that the price of aluminum is much too high. I am convinced that prices of oil and gasoline are altogether too high if, as is said by the engineers of the Department of Mines and Resources, we have-as they have shown -inexhaustible raw tar-sand resources from which to produce oil.
On February 18, 1942, the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) asked a question respecting the production of oil from tar sands. On that occasion the minister said:
lit indicates, however-
Referring to a report the minister had.
-that the location of the sands and the possibility of development is too remote to be of any great use in this war.
The war has been going on now for almost four years. We were in bad shape during the first year. What have we done since? What single thing have we done to relieve the oil shortage situation in this country? So far as I can see, extremely little has been done.
When on April 14 the minister opened his speech he said something I did not like, one, two, three:
There seems to be an erroneous idea in the minds of many regarding these tar sands. Whether these ideas are due to propaganda, supported by wishful thinking, I do not know.
It is neither propaganda nor wishful thinking upon which I base my arguments in connection with oil production. I base what I say upon thousands-no, I will not say thousands-but upon many miles of hard travel and survey, far into the Athabaska area. I have surveyed, myself, the tar sands there, and have carried out those surveys in the company of some of the greatest oil geologists in the world. One of them is very close to the top in Washington, and anything I have said

about tar sands and the possibilities of the production of oil has been 'based (1) on the reports issued by the government itself-and in my judgment, the Department of Mines and Resources has some of the ablest engineers in America, barring none, so far as understanding the development of oil from tar sands is concerned-(2) on reports of the United States bureau of mines, and the opinions of some of their best engineers and (3) my own observations, in company with engineers who travelled through that area. So that anything I say is not based on wishful thinking or propaganda. So far as I am concerned I am above propaganda. Others may speak for themselves, but I have long been convinced that the time has come for Canada to have a national oil policy, first, to make herself economically independent of any outside sources of oil supply and, second, to make us independent defensively.
What position are we in? If we were attacked by one of even the small nations, a nation which would have command of the air and oil supplies, we would be helpless. And we will continue to be so unless we wake up to the production of oil in Canada in a big way. There is no other way to save our people from the constant threat of lower gasoline rations, the constant threat to the owners of domestic oil-burner equipment, and the constant threat to our defence position.
I have already thanked the minister for sending investigators. However, I would not have sent the same investigators-and it will be understood I have nothing whatever to say against them. They were fine men, but I would have sent engineers from the Department of Mines and Resources. They were by far the better qualified.
They were up there, too.

They had surveyed the
area for thirty years, and they had drilled holes by the hundreds. Doctor S. C. Ells had traversed over two thousand miles through that area, drawing base lines. He has investigated numerous outcroppings, and had tested the sands in many places. In my judgment there is no better authority on tar sands than Doctor Ells.
Doctor Ells was in charge of the work there.

I was there, and I know
how little Doctor Ells had to do. I was there, and I make my own investigations. The engineers had been there for one month when I arrived, and up to that time as far as I know, they had little contact with Doctor Ells. If

the minister says they did have, then perhaps a parliamentary investigation will show just how little Doctor Ells had to do in carrying on the investigation of the tar sands area last summer.
I want to make statements which are based only on what I have seen with my own eyes and what I know from my own investigations.
I am not much for hearsay. I accept Doctor S. C. Ells' statement. In 1936 he made a statement to a mining engineering convention in Edmonton when he said that after exhaustive inquiry over many years it was his judgment that there were over 500 million barrels of oil available from the tar sands by open-cut method. This is mining that can be carried on *without too much trouble by removing the amount of top soil or none at all, and then [DOT]excavating the tar sand.
After 1936 a mill was built [DOT]costing around a million dollars and used to [DOT]develop this oil.
I am coming to that.
In 1942 the government tried to accelerate the inquiry. My hon. friend was in the house from 1930 to 1935.

I am coming to that.
That is what Doctor Ells said in 1936. Then last year he wrote an article for the June issue of the Canadian National Geographic magazine in which he stated that after further investigation, that would be between 1936 and 1942, he believed that a billion barrels of oil could be extracted by the open-cut method. The report presented by the minister is based on a six months investigation. I believe that during the first month of this investigation the proper equipment was not at hand to bore holes. Later on they used, I believe, Doctor Ells' equipment. The report submitted on April 14. 1943, stated in effect that approxi-mateb' 40 million barrels of oil were available by the open-cut method at Steep Bank and on the Horse river. Forty million barrels is a mere bagatelle to what should be there if the reports issued by the Department of Mines and Resources after thirty years investigation are correct. They should be correct. The Department of Mines and Resources should not send out reports based on thirty years investigation that are not correct. I, for one, believe them to be correct. I believe that there is a vast quantity of oil up there. As Doctor Ells says, there are a billion barrels which could be taken out by the open-cut method. And if some engineer should come along with an in situ method of extracting oil in those oil-sand areas where there is considerable top soil, Doctor Ells says that another
hundred billion barrels could be obtained. Surely someone will come along some day with a method which will save this country from being dependent on other countries for its supply of oil. With the proper method we would have available a hundred billion barrels, in addition to the billion barrels which Doctor Ells says can be taken out by the open-cut mothod. Doctor Ells is backed up by the mines and resources department engineers. I have talked to a number of them who have carried on investigations out there.
I made two trips to the Fort McMurray tar-sands area in 1941. On the first trip they were having difficulty with the mining. The sands were planed off with a revolving planer, and every now and then the knives of this planer would strike against a nodule, a round, heavy hard lump of the tar sand, and would break off. On the second trip they had adopted the powder-blasting method, and when I was there last summer, my third visit, they were still using this method and were finding it quite satisfactory. The report tabled by the minister states that as far as mining is concerned, it is very satisfactory. They have overcome one of the difficulties suggested by the minister.
Another argument against the development of the tar sands was that the extraction method is not satisfactory. As I said before, the engineers sent up last summer were good men, but I do not think they were there long enough to be able to make a report equal to that -made by the mines and resources department after thirty years. But even they stated that the method employed to separate the bitumen from the sand in the Abasand plant was satisfactory. We were told that two things were not satisfactory: First, mining -they say it is; second, the separation method-they say it is.
If these two things are satisfactory, and if the mines and resources department statement that there are inexhaustible quantities of oil in these sands is correct, I should like to know why the minister then fired the company which had been operating this plant. This company had done the pioneering work for the last few years; they had suffered everything but death in trying to keep the plant in operation. There may have been a shortage of money, and I presume there was or else they would have had a better plant. I should like to know why they were fired. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has been talking about a combine. Whom did the minister send up there to produce oil? He did not send outside engineers; oh, no. He sent members of the Canadian Oil company. He made the president of the Canadian Oil company the president of the

reorganized Abasand company. He made the vice-president and general manager of the Canadian Oil company the vice-president and general manager of the Abasand company. Two of the directors of the reorganized Abasand company are directors of the Canadian Oil company.
We want to get out of the hands of the big fellows. We want oil produced in this country and we want it produced at the right price. We have long paid too much for our oil; we have long paid far too much for our gasoline. I have nothing to say against these men, but I would feel more confident if the oil companies did not have a thing to do with the development of oil from these tar sands. I would much rather see this carried on by people who are not personally interested in oil.

Is my hon. friend suggesting that the Canadian Oil company is a great international cartel or anything of that sort? It is one of our smaller companies.
Mr. MaeNICOL: I do not suggest that, but I should like to know who are behind the Canadian Oil company. Are they connected with any other oil company?
Not that I know of.

No.

No.

It will be interesting to find out with whom they are associated. I have no fault to find with them, because they are fine men; but, as I say, I would be better pleased if the Canadian Oil company or any other company producing oil from wells did not have anything to do with the production of oil from these sands. I do not know much about the Abasand people. I met the president only twice and I have not seen him for most of a year, nor have I had any communication from him in that time. What I want to see is oil produced in this country.
I want to see this country released from being dependent upon any other country for its oil. We are told by the mines and resources department that the oil is there, and I take their word for it.
I am not going to say that the method of separation used by Abasand is perfect because I do not know enough about it. On the other hand I have made an exhaustive inquiry into oil, and I was extremely interested in reading 
the report of the United States senate investigating committee into the connection of the Standard Oil company with the production of rubber in Germany. I recommend every hon. member to read thoroughly this report. It tells all about the oil business, too. But I am perhaps a little ahead of my story and I will come back to that later.
The minister said at the conclusion of his remarks on April 14 that every known system had been tried. Let me quote his exact words, from page 2)153 of Hansard:
Every known process has been tried, and to-day I think the fact is that no satisfactory process either for mining the tar sands or for extracting the oil in an economical way has been wholly perfected.
I w'ould ask the minister if the Freeman process has been tried. Prior to 1935-36 the government of the day in Canada, or somebody acting for it, after consultation with Freeman, who is a great engineer and expert in the extraction of oil from low-grade coals and so forth, sent a lot of tar sands to London, where they were tested. I have the Freeman report in my hand. It is signed by himself and says in part:
The actual Freeman extraction method produced a total yield of 36-07 gallons per ton.
That is, from the tar sands which were-shipped over to England.
It goes on:
The oil lends itself easily to refining-
We have been told that it did not.
-and by the transformation refining method would produce motor spirit, lamp oil, lubricating bases and pitch.
That is out of the tar sands, from which he had extracted 36-07 gallons per ton. The-report goes on:
The above sands are surface sands but at a depth of thirty feet and more would in all probability produce as high as 75 gallons of excellent oil per ton by the extraction method.
I have the full story of the Freeman system here and have made careful inquiry into it.
1 should like to know later on if that system has been tried out. If not, then all known systems have not been tried.
I would ask further if the Blumner hydio-genization system was tried. The United States senate report gives an illuminating description of the wrhole oil business. From my studies I gather that in the early twenties a great engineer, Doctor Bergius, whose record I have here, invented the hydrogenization system. He was apparently not able to bring it to the point of operating in a commercial plant, but the great Doctor Blumner perfected the hydrogenization system to work in a commercial plant. Then the great German company I.G.

Farbenindustrie purchased Blumner patents and plant and proceeded to produce oil from coal. Doctor Blumner then, in collaboration with Doctor Fischer brought out his own Blumner process, which I presume he concluded was an improvement on the system which the Farbenindustrie was using. So far as I can understand, it was what I may call an improved Doctor Blumner process which the German government took over to use in the production of oil for Germany. When the war broke out, Germany was producing less than nine million barrels of oil a year, but they took over the Doctor Blumner process for extracting oil from coal by the hydro-genization method. When war broke out, it was thought that Germany would not be able to get enough gasoline for her war machine, but to-day Germany is producing 150 million barrels of gasoline a year aind1 since they conquered that part of Russia in the Donets Basin, they have built another plant there and are producing over ten million barrels a year there. If Germany can do it, why cannot we? Why should we be constantly threatened with having to throw out our domestic oil-burners which I understand would cost the country not less than fifty million dollars, including the coal-burning equipment that would have to be installed, and we cannot get the coal. If we have the oil resources we should have been producing the oil before this. As I said before, the oil controller has done a good job, but had we appointed an oil producer we could perhaps have dispensed with the services of the oil controller and got all the oil and gasoline for all our needs.
Someone asks what is hydrogenization. Mr. R. T. Haslam, a very great chemist with the Standard Oil company, described it in a very neat way. I quote from his evidence before the United States senate committee, at page 5040:
I want to explain just briefly and simply what hydrogenization is. In principle the process is simple; in practice it is complex.
I have here a lump of coal (exhibiting). I have in this bottle hydrogen (exhibiting). I could show' that it is hydrogen by touching a match to it. If there is no air in it it burns like the Hindenburg burned over Lakehurst, with a tough flame. If there happens to be a little air in it, it explodes. So therefore I will not demonstrate it to you.
The problem is how to get those tv'o together and combined chemically so that when v'e get through we have petroleum in this bottle (indicating). We convert a solid to a liquid. It is a matter of putting coal here (illustrating) plus hydrogen, and coming out with petroleum oil. That is done in complicated apparatus at a pressure of 3,500 pounds per square inch, at a temperature red hot, around 900 degrees Fahrenheit, and in the presence of hydrogen gas.
As I understand it, the hydrogen is introduced and acts as a catalyst and breaks down the molecules of oil in the coal. The oil is separated: from the coal, after the moisture has first been taken out of the coal. The place of the water is filled with other oil. The other oil is then recovered, too, and used over and over again. In his speech on April 14 the minister said the hydrogenization system would cost twelve million dollars. That is a small item. The minister has been doing a big job in many lines industrially, a marvellous job, and I know he could do just as big a job in the oil business if he would.
I appeal to him to go the limit in trying to produce oil in this country. If we cannot produce ample oil from the tar sands-but I believe wre can-we can produce oil from coal. We have lots of coal in Nova Scotia and Saskatchewan and mountains of it in Alberta, from which we could produce all the oil that is required. If we have the will to produce the oil we can lift this country out of the position we are in now and be defensively and economically independent so far as oil is concerned, instead of being under this constant threat of a shortage.
The government could put up a pilot plant and demonstrate that oil can be extracted from coal. All these systems, the Freeman, the Blumner and the I. G. Farbenindustrie extract oil from coal, but they can extract oil from tar-sand bitumen, too.
Doctor Thau was one of the greatest oil engineers in Germany. The German government appointed him to look into the Blumner process, and I have here a copy of his report in which he gives a description of this process. I will quote a paragraph:
Coal in the pulverized state, is mixed with about an equal quantity of oil with high boiling point, and the mixture after having passed through a heat exchanger is under elevated pressure forced through this set of six retorts in a series at comparatively high rate of velocity. The retorts are connected to each other by a pipe leading from the outlet at the top of one of the retorts to the bottom inlet of the next. These connecting pipes are passed vertically through the heated brick setting to prevent a loss of heat of the fuel in its way from one retort to the next.
This report to the German government, I am informed, was the basis upon which they accepted the process to produce oil, and the fact that they are producing 150 million barrels a year speaks volumes in his favour. I would support the minister to the limit if he would introduce a bill, asking for whatever sum of money he might consider necessary for the purpose of putting up a hydrogenization plant in Canada to produce oil either from our coal or from our tar sands or from our torbanites or from our hydro carbons of any kind.

So far as I am concerned. I am not talking politics. This is no time to talk politics, and I am a Canadian above everything else.
I know that'. I simply wanted to be sure that you could be in the house.

Should we not try to get ourselves out of that trap if we possibly can? If we could produce oil and gasoline on a large scale we would get our gas at a much lower rate and our citizens would have oil to bum in their furnaces. If our gasoline ration goes any lower and if Canadians are compelled to take out their oil-burners in that event-I am not blaming the minister-someone	will be
responsible. Why not let us act upon the reports we have received from our own Department of Mines and Resources, who have been investigating the situation for the last thirty years? In that department we have had some of the best engineers in this field; they have studied the question of oil production, and on the basis of their investigations we are given to understand that our requirements could be satisfied. The minister said that a hydrogenization mill could be put up for $12,000,000 to produce 20,000 barrels a day. If you put up 4 mills that would be around $50,000,000 and that would give you another
60,000	barrels a day. That would make us, together with what is now produced, independent of any other country, both economically and from the point of view of defence.
Something was said about sulphur. In this connection I was alarmed at some of the remarks the minister made because I thought I knew a little about chemistry and the question of desulphurization. He said, with regard to the question of desulphurizing oil obtained

from bitumen and tar sands, that a percentage-of sulphur remained after the process. I had always believed that a wash sulphuric acid" and caustic soda would desulphurize anything that contained sulphur, and for this reason I wrote to one of the great companies of the United States with a view to obtaining some information on the subject. I got in touch with the Phillips Petroleum company. They did not stipulate that I should not quote from their letter and I do not think it would do any harm. The letter is not marked con* fidential. They say:
Although the sulphur in the crude oil as extracted from the oil sands may be as high as 5 per cent, it seems unlikely that there would be more than a few tenths of one per cent in the lighter products, such as motor fuel, manufactured from the oil. High sulphur content in the heavier products, such as asphalt or fuel oil, is of little importance.
The circulars enclosed tell about the process w'hich they use for extracting sulphur from crude oil. I learned also from a number of oil companies that a great many varieties of crude oil contain sulphur. So that the sulphur content is not as serious a problem as it appears to be.
Let me say this in conclusion, Mr. Chairman. In connection with any investigations I have made with regard to oil or anything else and which I have submitted to this house I have had no other object before me than the desire to render some service to my native-land. I have always tried to do that to the best of my ability. As I said at the commencement of my remarks, I have believed, and I still believe, that we have in Alberta a product which we should develop and of which we should avail ourselves. The Turner valley produces 8,000,000 barrels; and if we take all the wells in Canada, including the Turner valley, we have a production of from 10,000,000' to 12,000.000 barrels a year. This means that we must import from 80,000,000 to 90,000,000' barrels more. It is the duty of Canadians, therefore, to make every effort to find somewhere in Canada sufficient oil to make up the difference between what is now produced and what is required; and if we cannot get it from oil wells, of which there are thousands throughout the country, there is no reason why we should not get it from the source I have already indicated. The average oil field produces 9,000 barrels per acre, whereas, according to Doctor Ells, the tar sands contain
70,000	barrels per acre. I suggest to the minister that he should send up some men from the Department of Mines and Resources to investigate and report to him, and on that basis he could bring in a bill for the erection of hydrogenization plants. The minister knows
